questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A detail that is not incidental
questions.learningObjective: Identify a detail that functions as evidence rather than as decoration
questions.stem: One tank note describes a small crab as left-clawed, permanently, in a tank where nothing had ever been able to pinch it. What does the detail chiefly do?

options.text: It records a harmless oddity of the specimen, which has no bearing on the notes around it.
options.misconception: dismisses a detail the note makes conspicuous

options.text: It turns a physical trait into evidence about the animal's history inside the tank.
It establishes the biologist's taste for detail, since the trait is described in detail.
options.misconception: takes description of a trait as evidence of the writer

options.text: It warns that the specimen is aggressive and should be handled with more care.
options.misconception: reads a trait as a safety instruction

questions.explanation: The claw is introduced with the fact that nothing in the tank could have caused it, which turns a physical trait into a record of the animal's history. Incidental oddity, a display of the writer's thoroughness, and a warning each miss what the note actually argues.
questions.hint: Ask why the note mentions what the tank could not do.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a small observational detail carries real information
questions.stem: One tank note records that the small crab took the brine shrimp before the large one had finished moving toward them. Explain why the detail about who ate first is not incidental.

answer.exemplar: The order of feeding is a record of behaviour, not of decoration, and the note is careful about it because the size difference between the two animals would normally settle the question in advance. The small crab's priority therefore tells the biologist something about the animals' appetites and about how the tank's hierarchy actually works in practice, which is exactly what the notes exist to record. A detail like this is incidental only when it carries no information; here it is the evidence, and the whole entry would be weaker if the biologist had simply written that both animals fed.

questions.explanation: The order of feeding is behavioural evidence, especially because the larger animal would normally be expected to feed first, so the detail carries information rather than decoration. Without it the entry would record only that both animals fed.
questions.hint: Ask what the order tells the biologist.

questions.explanation: The stated reason makes the slower instrument a choice made for the specimens' sake, which is what the decision reveals about the biologist's priorities. Timidity, inefficiency, and distrust each substitute a motive the note explicitly rules out.

options.misconception: reduces the relationship to competition for food

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A foil identified in a passage
questions.learningObjective: Explain how two adjacent sentences work as a foil against one another
questions.stem: Two consecutive entries in a marine biologist's tank notes describe a wrasse and a goby feeding. The first says the wrasse takes food from the tank floor within a second of it landing. The second says the goby waits under the sand until the food has been carried off. Explain how the second sentence functions against the first.

answer.exemplar: The first sentence establishes the wrasse as immediate and unhesitating, and the second places the goby in deliberate contrast, waiting while the food is carried away. Because the two are described in adjacent sentences and under the same conditions, the reader receives a comparison without being told one is being made, which is the usual way a foil operates in a passage. The contrast sharpens both animals rather than simply opposing them: the wrasse looks bold partly because the goby looks cautious. Read on its own, the second sentence would be a bare observation; read against the first, it carries the passage's argument about temperament.

questions.explanation: Placed in adjacent sentences under the same conditions, the goby's waiting is set against the wrasse's speed, so the contrast sharpens both animals. The foil works by comparison the notes never have to state.
questions.hint: Ask what the second sentence looks like beside the first.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a description of a general kind reads as flat
questions.stem: One reef fish is described in a marine biologist's tank notes as a fish of the usual sort, medium size, and no more interesting than its neighbours. Explain why such a description reads as flat.

answer.exemplar: The description assigns the fish attributes that are true of nearly every fish of its kind, so a reader learns nothing that distinguishes this individual from its neighbours. Flatness in a character description comes from this: the particulars offered are all general, and no choice, habit, or private concern attaches to the animal. The notes are not written to entertain, so the description is not a failure of the form; it is a record in which the entry for this animal carries no distinctive information. The round alternative would have noticed something about this fish in particular, as the notes do for the others.

questions.explanation: Every attribute given could apply to any fish of its kind, so nothing distinguishes this individual, which is what flatness means in a description. The round entries in the same notes single out habits and choices particular to one animal.
questions.hint: Ask what is true only of this animal.

questions.stem: One mirror left in a marine biologist's tank notes is explained in the entry itself: a colony without a mirror is not the colony the writer is trying to describe. Explain what the choice reveals about the biologist.

answer.exemplar: The biologist has chosen to describe the colony as it actually behaves, mirror and all, rather than as it would look in isolation, and the reason given makes this a claim about honesty of method rather than about modesty. A reader can infer a lot from it: the biologist cares about what the specimen is rather than about how it might present, and understands that the mirror is part of the social situation being observed. The choice is therefore a small piece of evidence about character, because it reveals a priority. A note that simply described the colony's behaviour without the mirror would tell the reader what happened but not what the biologist thought mattered.

questions.explanation: The mirror is kept deliberately so the colony is described as it is, which reveals a priority for truth in the record rather than for a tidier specimen. A note without the mirror would report behaviour but not what the biologist considered important.

questions.stem: One disturbed patch of gravel and a hole under a pipe are recorded in a marine biologist's tank notes. Explain why the mention of the hole is not incidental.

answer.exemplar: The disturbed gravel is a sign and the hole is the evidence of what made it, so the detail is what upgrades a suspicion into something the notes can act on. A biologist who wrote only that the gravel looked disturbed would leave the reader with an impression; the hole gives a measurable feature, and features are what a record is for. This is the ordinary way the small particulars of an observation carry the argument: nothing in the sentence announces that it matters, but remove the hole and the entry has nothing to report. The detail is also the point at which the note becomes usable for someone else reading it months later.

questions.explanation: The hole is the evidence that turns a suspicion into a checkable observation, so it is the reason the entry has any value. Without it the note asks the reader to take a disturbance on trust.

options.misconception: reads a behavioural tempo as a fault

options.text: The description criticises the biologist's own methods, since one animal was watched in isolation.
options.misconception: turns a single description into a methodological complaint

questions.explanation: The jellyfish's slowness becomes legible only against the tank's quicker animals, so the description opens a comparison the notes develop elsewhere. A fault, an isolated watch, and a complaint about method each read the sentence in ways the text does not support.
questions.hint: Ask what the tank's other animals are needed for.

questions.learningObjective: Identify what a contrasted pair of columns asks the reader to weigh

options.text: It sets a test, since the two columns are about to be used as experimental conditions.
options.misconception: reads the columns as an experiment

options.text: It sets a hierarchy, since the page measures which animal is the stronger of the two.
options.misconception: reads the columns as a ranking of dominance

options.text: It sets a contrast whose meaning the last line asks the reader to weigh and decide.

questions.explanation: The two columns present contrasting habits, and the final line invites the reader to judge which animal the biologist means, so the passage is built on a comparison the reader must weigh. Rivalry, an experiment, and a hierarchy each add structures the page does not contain.

options.misconception: turns a stated absence into a hidden event

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a trade-off recorded in a note reveals a value
questions.stem: One marking decision is explained in a marine biologist's tank notes, with speed traded against accuracy. Explain what the choice reveals about the biologist.

answer.exemplar: The biologist has traded speed for a claim about accuracy, and has said so in the note, which is unusual because most choices in these logs go unremarked. That makes the decision a small piece of evidence about method and about values: this person would rather do a task properly and slowly than do it quickly and approximately. The reader can also infer a humility about the limits of marking, since a painted number is a claim about identity that the biologist is unwilling to make from the end of a net. Character in these notes is built out of choices like this one, made under ordinary pressures and then noted.

questions.explanation: The biologist trades speed for accuracy and says so, which reveals a preference for doing a task properly over doing it quickly. Such noted choices build character in these logs more reliably than self-description would.
questions.hint: Ask what the slower method was worth to the biologist.

questions.learningObjective: Judge whether a description makes an animal particular

options.text: It is flat, since no measurement of the animal's behaviour is given.
options.misconception: demands quantities from a character description

It is neither, since the note is really about the biologist's feelings rather than the animal.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how two contrasted descriptions make each other clearer
questions.stem: Two entries in a marine biologist's tank notes describe a stonefish that has never moved and been never touched, and a lionfish that has moved eleven times and been touched twice, both times by accident. Comparing the two, which claim holds up best?

options.text: The two descriptions show the same kind of animal recorded with opposite habits, so neither serves as a contrast.
options.misconception: denies the contrast the descriptions set up

options.text: Each description measures the other, and the pair makes stillness and activity vivid against each other.
The stonefish is a foil for the lionfish, since the second description's count depends on the first.
options.misconception: fixes a direction the pairing does not need

options.text: The pair is only a practical record, since counts of movement are standard in these notes.
options.misconception: dismisses the comparison as routine bookkeeping

questions.explanation: The two entries set immobility against repeated activity, and each description makes the other more vivid, which is what a foil arrangement does. A shared kind, a fixed direction, and routine bookkeeping each miss the comparative work the pair performs.
questions.hint: Ask what each description makes clearer about the other.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A detail that is not incidental
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a piece of physical evidence earns its place in a record
questions.stem: A small shape under a filter intake is found and left undisturbed in a marine biologist's tank notes, where the writer gives as the reason that it was settled and had chosen the spot. Explain why that detail is not incidental.

answer.exemplar: The detail is not incidental because where an animal settles is the information the note is gathering, and the biologist declines to disturb it precisely so the observation stays undisturbed. The stated reason also reveals something about the practice behind the record: a keeper who could have looked and chose not to is making a different choice from one who never thought of it. Such notes are full of small permissions and refusals, and they are the material from which a reader builds a picture of how the work is done. Without the detail there would be only a sighting, and with it there is a decision.

questions.explanation: The detail records not just a sighting but a decision to leave it undisturbed, so it carries information about both the animal and the practice. Without it there would be only a sighting, and with it there is a decision.
questions.hint: Ask what the refusal to disturb it records.

questions.hint: Ask what the three figures add up to.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the shift in attitude that a change of plan reveals

stimulus.body: From the tank notes, an entry with a decision written into it: The blue tang has been eating the corals for a fortnight and I have been moving it to the other end of the tank each time, which fixes it for a day and does not fix it at all. questions.stem: Consider the tank note printed here, in which a blue tang's habits lead to a change of plan. Which judgement best describes what the choice reveals?

options.text: It shows a biologist who enjoys conflict, since moving the fish has become a daily event.
options.misconception: infers enjoyment from a repeated chore

options.text: It shows a biologist who is attached to the fish and cannot part with it.
options.misconception: invents attachment the note does not express

options.text: It shows a biologist who is convinced the corals can be saved by better positioning.
options.misconception: reads a habit as a conviction about the method

options.text: It shows a biologist who has stopped trying to prevent a behaviour and wants to understand it instead.

questions.explanation: The repeated moving is acknowledged as ineffective and the next step is to separate the fish and observe it freely, so the choice reveals a shift from control to understanding. Enjoyment, attachment, and confidence in positioning each miss that shift.

options.text: The descriptions form a contrast of methods, and each one makes the other easier to understand.
